claims.text: The starting material is a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without yttrium or other secondary reactive elements.
The intervention is to add 1–2 at% yttrium to CoCrFeNi during synthesis.
Mechanical alloying, hot isostatic pressing, and calibrated annealing can produce the proposed yttrium-modified alloy.
Adding 1–2 at% yttrium to CoCrFeNi will cause in situ formation of uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoprecipitates.
The modified alloy will have an ultrafine-grained matrix pinned by Y2O3 nanoprecipitates.
At lower temperatures, the nanoprecipitates will inhibit grain coarsening through Zener pinning.
Suppression of grain coarsening will maintain high hardness and strength during low-temperature sliding.
At high temperatures, pre-dispersed oxides will promote tribochemical reactions and formation of a protective adaptive oxide glaze.
The high-temperature glaze will be continuous, lubricious, and nanocrystalline.
The oxide glaze will reduce adhesive and oxidative wear during high-temperature sliding.
Y2O3-related grain refinement can increase oxide nucleation, refine oxidation products, and improve oxide-layer adhesion and stability.
The yttrium-modified alloy will have a lower coefficient of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The coefficient of friction may remain below 0.3 throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The modified alloy may sustain a specific wear rate of approximately 10^-7–10^-6 mm³/N-m from room temperature to 800 °C.
Sliding performance is to be evaluated from room temperature to 800 °C under a normal load of 10–20 N.
Using a controlled dry or low-oxygen environment will minimize variability from external oxidation.
Variation in yttrium dispersion and precipitate size could alter the consistency of the proposed grain-pinning and oxide-glaze mechanisms.
A controlled comparison will use yttrium-modified and yttrium-free CoCrFeNi samples processed and tested identically.
TEM and atom-probe tomography will be used to test whether the intended Y2O3 dispersion and size distribution were achieved.

The hypothesis is falsified if the modified alloy both fails to maintain coefficient of friction below 0.3 and fails to reduce wear rate by at least one order of magnitude relative to the control across the full temperature range.

contradictions.description: The proposed high-temperature protection depends on oxidation and tribochemical formation of an oxide glaze, while testing is specified in a low-oxygen environment intended to suppress external oxidation. The minimum oxygen activity needed for glaze formation is not defined, so the boundary may inhibit the proposed mechanism.
